     17	metadata:
     18	  author: dewavic
     19	  version: "1.0.0"
     20	  summary: "Troubleshoot Amazon EBS performance, volume modifications, snapshots, encryption, quotas and cost, and review an account's EBS setup with read-only checks."
     21	  aws-devops-agent-skills.agent-types: "CHAT, INCIDENT_RCA"
     22	  aws-devops-agent-skills.aws-services: "Amazon EBS, Amazon EC2, Amazon CloudWatch, AWS CloudTrail, AWS Service Quotas"

     24	---
     25	# Amazon EBS Expertise
     26	
     27	Use this skill to troubleshoot Amazon EBS problems and to review an account's Amazon EBS setup. It has two modes. Troubleshoot mode answers "something is wrong, why?" through one of five paths and returns a fixed verdict. Review mode answers "is my EBS setup healthy before something goes wrong?" and returns a rated report. Both modes are read-only and share the same volume-type rules, instance limits and service rules. Load only the reference files the request needs.
     28	
     29	## When to Use This Skill
     30	
     31	- Storage-related slowness, timeouts or high I/O latency on an Amazon EC2 instance.
     32	- An alarm on AWS/EBS metrics or on instance `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%`.
     33	- A request to raise IOPS or throughput, or to modify a volume.
     34	- A volume modification that looks stuck, failed, or did not improve performance.
     35	- Snapshot, AMI, Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager, AWS Backup or Recycle Bin questions, including which snapshots need owner review before deletion.
     36	- Encrypted-volume access errors and AWS KMS questions for Amazon EBS.
     37	- Amazon EBS cost increases, idle or over-provisioned volumes.
     38	- An operation that failed on an Amazon EBS quota, or "how close am I to my limits?"
     39	- A request to review Amazon EBS posture before a launch, migration or peak event.
     40	
     41	Do not use this skill for Amazon S3, Amazon EFS, Amazon FSx, instance store, or Amazon EC2 issues unrelated to Amazon EBS.
     42	
     43	## Prerequisites
     44	
     45	- Read-only permissions for the APIs listed in [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md).
     46	- AWS CloudTrail access is optional. The skill works without it.
     47	- Mutating changes run only through directed actions (Agent Actions in the Operator Web App), which need their own role and operator approval on the approval card.
     48	
     49	---
     50	
     51	## Workflow
     52	
     53	Copy this checklist and tick each step as you finish it:
     54	
     55	- [ ] Step 1: Classify the request
     56	- [ ] Step 2: Load the shared references
     57	- [ ] Step 3: Run the path and draft the report
     58	- [ ] Step 4: Check the draft, fix it, then present it
     59	
     60	## Step 1: Classify the Request
     61	
     62	| The user says or the alarm shows | Mode and path | Load |
     63	|---|---|---|
     64	| "My app is slow", high latency, an alarm on AWS/EBS metrics, `EBSIOBalance%` or `EBSByteBalance%`, "is it storage?", "how much IOPS do I need?" | Troubleshoot: performance | [references/troubleshoot-performance.md](references/troubleshoot-performance.md) |
     65	| "My modification is stuck", "the new IOPS has not taken effect", a `ModifyVolume` error, resize, gp2 to gp3, extend the file system, shrink or cancel | Troubleshoot: volume modification | [references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md](references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md) |
     66	| "Which snapshots can I delete?", snapshot copy did not arrive, AMI creation stuck, recover a deleted snapshot or volume, Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager, Recycle Bin | Troubleshoot: snapshots | [references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md](references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md) |
     67	| "I can't attach my KMS-encrypted volume", share an encrypted snapshot or AMI, encryption by default, re-encrypt a volume | Troubleshoot: encryption | [references/troubleshoot-encryption.md](references/troubleshoot-encryption.md) |
     68	| "Why did my EBS bill go up?", unexplained charges, idle or unattached volumes, pricing model | Troubleshoot: billing | [references/troubleshoot-billing.md](references/troubleshoot-billing.md) |
     69	| "Limit exceeded", a quota error, "how close am I to my limits?" | Shared capability: quota headroom | [Capacity and quota headroom](references/review-operational.md#capacity-and-quota-headroom) |
     70	| "Are my volumes backed up?" | Review: resilience area | [Resilience](references/review-operational.md#resilience) |
     71	| "Review my EBS setup", "is my storage production-ready?" | Review | [references/review-operational.md](references/review-operational.md) and [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md) |
     72	
     73	If a request fits more than one row, answer the question the user asked first and treat the rest as Separate findings.
     74	
     75	## Step 2: Load the Shared References
     76	
     77	- Always load [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md) (read-only APIs, metric math, errors and fallbacks).
     78	- Load [references/metrics-thresholds.md](references/metrics-thresholds.md) for any metric judgement.
     79	- Load [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md) for the verdict, the binding layer, escalation and review ratings.
     80	- Load [references/ebs-best-practices.md](references/ebs-best-practices.md) for service rules (Elastic Volumes, instance limits, quotas, snapshots, quirks).
     81	
     82	## Step 3: Run the Path and Draft the Report
     83	
     84	Follow the numbered procedure in the loaded path. Discover every value from the APIs. Then draft the report in the format below.
     85	
     86	### Troubleshoot verdict format
     87	
     88	1. **Answer:** the asked question, answered first.
     89	2. **Evidence:** values with units and time window.
     90	3. **Binding layer:** Volume, Instance, Burst credits, Quota, Not EBS, AWS-side impairment (only with a direct signal, see [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md)), Indeterminate, or Not applicable.
     91	4. **Recommendation:** exact parameters, or "No change".
     92	5. **Separate findings:** other true facts that do not change the Answer.
     93	6. **Gaps:** what could not be checked and why.
     94	
     95	In an investigation, put the Answer and the Recommendation with its exact parameters in the root cause finding, not only under Gaps. Keep the findings on the resource the user asked about. Mention another volume only when it shares the same instance EBS baseline, and then as a Separate finding.
     96	
     97	When the Binding layer is Indeterminate, report it as one finding. Do not offer AWS-side impairment as a hypothesis. List each direct check you ran (volume status, `VolumeStalledIOCheck`, AWS Health, AWS FIS) with its result as supporting evidence, say that no check confirms or rules out an EBS-side slowdown, and give the escalation path.
     98	
     99	Review mode uses the rated report in [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md). Every Review mode response MUST begin with its Summary table, which rates all six areas (capacity and quota headroom, observability, cost hygiene, resilience, encryption posture, deletion protection), even when an area has no findings or is `Indeterminate`. The Summary table is required, not optional. Do not open with prose or an offer to run the review; start with the table, then the per-area detail.
     100	
     101	## Step 4: Check the Draft Before Presenting It
     102	
     103	Review the draft from Step 3 against these checks. Fix anything that fails, then present it.
     104	
     105	- Every number under Evidence came from an API call made in this session, has its unit and time window, and matches the resource ID it is attributed to.
     106	- The Binding layer agrees with the Evidence: the named layer is the one at its limit, and the other layers were checked and shown to have headroom. The Evidence gives the instance EBS baseline in MiB/s and IOPS next to the summed demand of all attached volumes.
     107	- Any Recommendation stays within the instance's EBS baseline and the volume type's documented limits, and it is not more provisioning for an impairment.
     108	- Every snapshot tier is backed by the checks it requires; if one of those checks failed, the item is not listed for owner review. No snapshot is recommended for deletion; the owner confirms first.
     109	- A review answer starts with the Summary table and rates all six areas.
     110	- Every API that failed or was not called is listed under Gaps.
     111	
     112	---
     113	
     114	## Critical Rules
     115	
     116	- **Read-only.** Changes (ModifyVolume, quota requests) are proposed with exact parameters, cost and rollback, and run only through operator-approved directed actions (Agent Actions in the Operator Web App). Approval is given only on the approval card. A typed "approve" in chat is not approval.
     117	- **Deletes are manual customer steps.** AWS DevOps Agent refuses delete-class operations (for example DeleteSnapshot, DeleteVolume, DeregisterImage), so never propose them as directed actions. After the owner confirms they no longer need the resource, give the commands for the customer to run with their own credentials.
     118	- **Answer in one reply.** In chat, run the checks in this conversation and return the finished verdict or report as your reply. Do not hand the work to a background sub-agent and reply with a "started" or "I will report back" message, because that message becomes the answer the user sees first.
     119	- **Discover, don't assume:** read every configuration value from the APIs.
     120	- **Rule EBS in or out before tuning it.**
     121	- **Answer the asked question first;** other findings go under "Separate findings".
     122	- **Review mode starts with the Summary table.** Every Review mode response begins with the Summary table of all six rated areas. The table is required, not optional.
     123	- **Always check the instance layer** and size changes within the instance's EBS **baseline**.
     124	- **Never recommend more provisioning for an impairment.**
     125	- **Use current service rules:** up to 4 Elastic Volumes modifications per volume per rolling 24 hours. There is no fixed waiting period between modifications; the next one is allowed once the previous one completes.
     126	- **No interpretation without data:** report what couldn't be checked and use fallbacks. `DescribeVolumesModifications` returns only the most recent modification per volume; modification history and counts come from the optional AWS CloudTrail `ModifyVolume` events, or are listed under Gaps.
     127	- **Units:** MiB/s for throughput, stated every time.
     128	- **Escalate** on scope signals or when the investigation can't explain the symptom.
     129	
     130	## Gotchas
     131	
     132	- A modification in `optimizing` is not stuck. The new size, IOPS or throughput already applies while it optimizes.
     133	- `DescribeInstanceTypes` reports EBS bandwidth in MB/s. Convert it to MiB/s before comparing it with volume throughput.
     134	- On io1 and io2, `VolumeThroughputPercentage` is the percentage of provisioned IOPS delivered. It is not a throughput signal.
     135	- `VolumeAvgIOPS`, `VolumeAvgThroughput`, `VolumeAvgReadLatency` and `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` need both `VolumeId` and `InstanceId` and exist only on Nitro instances. `VolumeAvgThroughput` is in KiB/s. `VolumeTotalReadTime` and `VolumeTotalWriteTime` are in seconds.
     136	- Rising latency and queue length with falling IOPS is not proof of an AWS-side impairment. Without a direct signal (failed `VolumeStalledIOCheck`, impaired volume status, or an open AWS Health event) and without a running AWS FIS experiment, the Binding layer is Indeterminate.
     137	- `DescribeVolumesModifications` returns only the latest modification per volume. It cannot count modifications in the last 24 hours.
     138	- `ListRecoveryPointsByResource` without `ManagedByAWSBackupOnly` set to true also lists snapshots that AWS Backup did not create.
     139	- A snapshot whose source volume is gone may be the only remaining copy of the data. List it for owner review; never call it safe to delete.
     140	- Snapshots are incremental, so deleting one may free less storage than its size suggests.
     141	
     142	## Error Handling
     143	
     144	Errors, gated reads and missing metrics are handled with the fallback table in [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md). Name every failed API under Gaps and continue with the rest.
     145	
     146	## References
     147	
     148	- [references/troubleshoot-performance.md](references/troubleshoot-performance.md): performance attribution, the live-tested procedure
     149	- [references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md](references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md): snapshot tiers (owner review), copy, AMI, lifecycle and recovery
     150	- [references/troubleshoot-encryption.md](references/troubleshoot-encryption.md): AWS KMS access, sharing encrypted snapshots, default encryption
     151	- [references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md](references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md): modification states, limits, errors, sizing, file system extension
     152	- [references/troubleshoot-billing.md](references/troubleshoot-billing.md): cost breakdown, change records, right-sizing
     153	- [references/review-operational.md](references/review-operational.md): Review mode checks and the quota headroom capability
     154	- [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md): read-only API allowlist, metric math, errors, fallbacks
     155	- [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md): verdict template, binding layer, escalation, review ratings
     156	- [references/metrics-thresholds.md](references/metrics-thresholds.md): documented limits and how to judge each volume type
     157	- [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md): rated report layout for Review mode
     158	- [references/ebs-best-practices.md](references/ebs-best-practices.md): volume-type rules, quotas, Elastic Volumes rules, quirks"}], "status": "success", "type": "tool_result"}], "user_reference": null}

{"id": "3adae90b-79ef-42a5-a532-650960a5c636", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_xLjUnA3k9RJOstPANBt93V", "content": [{"text": "     1	# Troubleshoot: performance attribution
     2	
     3	## When this path applies
     4	
     5	- The user reports slowness, timeouts or high I/O latency on an instance or application.
     6	- A CloudWatch alarm fired on AWS/EBS metrics (`VolumeReadOps`, `VolumeWriteOps`, `VolumeReadBytes`, `VolumeWriteBytes`, `VolumeQueueLength`, `VolumeTotalReadTime`, `VolumeTotalWriteTime`, `VolumeAvgIOPS`, `VolumeAvgThroughput`, `BurstBalance`) or on instance `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%`.
     7	- A volume modification did not improve performance.
     8	- The user asks how much IOPS or throughput to provision.
     9	
     10	## Procedure
     11	
     12	Discover everything from the alarm. Do not assume volume type, size, provisioned values, instance type, or tags; read them from the APIs.
     13	
     14	### Step 1: Identify the alarmed volume(s)
     15	
     16	- Get the alarm and its state history (when it first entered ALARM).
     17	- Extract VolumeId from the alarm's metric dimensions. For metric-math alarms, read the VolumeId from each metric in the expression.
     18	- If the alarm is on an instance metric (EBSIOBalance%, EBSByteBalance%), start from the InstanceId instead.
     19	- If there is no alarm (a chat request such as "my app is slow"), start from the InstanceId the user gives, or ask for it.
     20	
     21	### Step 2: Build the context
     22	
     23	- DescribeVolumes on the alarmed volume: VolumeType, Size, Iops, Throughput, attachment InstanceId, tags (for naming only).
     24	- DescribeInstances + DescribeInstanceTypes for that instance: instance type and its EBS baseline/maximum bandwidth (MiB/s) and IOPS.
     25	- List ALL volumes attached to that instance (they share instance EBS bandwidth). Investigate this set, not the whole account.
     26	- `DescribeInstanceTypes` reports throughput in MB/s. Convert to MiB/s before any comparison (see [data-collection.md](data-collection.md)).
     27	- Always run `DescribeVolumeStatus` for every attached volume (volume status, status checks, scheduled events), whatever the alarm or request. Record the result as evidence. An impaired status or a failing check is a scope signal for escalation (see [finding-logic.md](finding-logic.md)), but still finish Steps 3 to 5.
     28	
     29	### Step 2b: Rule EBS in or out (chat requests with no EBS alarm only)
     30	
     31	This check runs only when the run did not start from an AWS/EBS alarm or an `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%` alarm, for example a chat request such as "my app is slow, is it storage?". When an EBS alarm triggered the run, skip this step and run Steps 3 to 6 in full.
     32	
     33	Read `CPUUtilization` for the instance, and the latency, `VolumeQueueLength`, `BurstBalance` (gp2, st1, sc1) and instance `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%` (if published) for the volumes found in Step 2, over the same window. Use the qualitative attribution matrix in [finding-logic.md](finding-logic.md). Report "Not EBS" and stop tuning storage only if all of these hold: CPU is high, volume latency and queue length are normal, no `DescribeVolumeStatus` problem was found, and no burst or instance balance is draining or at 0. Otherwise continue with Step 3.
     34	
     35	### Step 3: Measure each volume on the dimension(s) its type is limited by
     36	
     37	Pull the last 30 minutes of AWS/EBS metrics at 1-minute granularity.
     38	
     39	- Actual IOPS = (VolumeReadOps + VolumeWriteOps) / period seconds
     40	- Actual throughput = (VolumeReadBytes + VolumeWriteBytes) / period, in MiB/s
     41	- Avg latency in ms per operation = Sum(VolumeTotalReadTime) / Sum(VolumeReadOps) x 1,000, and the same for writes with VolumeTotalWriteTime and VolumeWriteOps. VolumeTotalReadTime and VolumeTotalWriteTime are in seconds, so the x 1,000 converts to milliseconds. `VolumeAvgReadLatency` and `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` are already in milliseconds
     42	- VolumeQueueLength
     43	- `VolumeAvgIOPS`, `VolumeAvgThroughput`, `VolumeAvgReadLatency` and `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` need both dimensions, `VolumeId` AND `InstanceId`, and exist only on Nitro instances. `VolumeAvgThroughput` is in KiB/s; divide by 1,024 for MiB/s. `VolumeQueueLength` uses `VolumeId` only. If `VolumeAvg*` returns nothing, use the Sum-based math above.
     44	- Always read `VolumeIdleTime` (seconds in the period with no read or write submitted; `VolumeId` only). Idle percentage = Sum(`VolumeIdleTime`) / period seconds x 100. Report it as evidence for every volume. Near 0 means I/O was submitted for the whole period, which fits both saturation and impairment, so use Step 5 to tell them apart. A volume that is mostly idle during the alarm window is unlikely to be the binding volume. There is no fixed band; compare with the volume's own history.
     45	
     46	Apply the rule for the volume's type:
     47	
     48	- gp3: IOPS and throughput are provisioned independently. Compare actual IOPS to Iops AND actual MiB/s to Throughput; either can bind.
     49	- gp2: baseline IOPS = 3 x GiB (min 100), burst to 3,000 while BurstBalance > 0. Check BurstBalance draining or at 0.
     50	- io1/io2 (incl. Block Express): compare actual IOPS to provisioned Iops AND actual MiB/s to the volume's throughput limit; either can bind. Throughput is not provisioned separately, but the documented throughput limit depends on the provisioned IOPS (see the io1 and io2 rows in [metrics-thresholds.md](metrics-thresholds.md)).      22	Nothing outside this list is called by the skill on its own. Mutating calls are proposals (see SKILL.md Critical rules).
     23	
     24	## Metric rules
     25	
     26	AWS/EBS publishes 1-minute data.
     27	
     28	| Namespace | Metrics | Dimensions |
     29	|---|---|---|
     30	| AWS/EBS | `VolumeAvgIOPS` (Ops/s), `VolumeAvgThroughput` (KiB/s), `VolumeAvgReadLatency` (milliseconds), `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` (milliseconds), `VolumeStalledIOCheck` (0 passed, 1 failed) | `VolumeId` AND `InstanceId`. Nitro instances only |
     31	| AWS/EBS | `VolumeReadOps`, `VolumeWriteOps`, `VolumeReadBytes`, `VolumeWriteBytes`, `VolumeTotalReadTime` (seconds), `VolumeTotalWriteTime` (seconds), `VolumeQueueLength`, `VolumeIdleTime` (seconds), `BurstBalance`, `VolumeThroughputPercentage` (Provisioned IOPS SSD only) | `VolumeId` |
     32	| AWS/EC2 | `EBSIOBalance%`, `EBSByteBalance%`, `EBSReadOps`, `EBSWriteOps`, `EBSReadBytes`, `EBSWriteBytes` | `InstanceId` |
     33	
     34	Metric math from the Amazon CloudWatch metrics page for Amazon EBS. Use `Sum` statistics for ops, bytes and time.
     35	
     36	- IOPS = Sum(`VolumeReadOps` + `VolumeWriteOps`) / period in seconds
     37	- MiB/s = Sum(`VolumeReadBytes` + `VolumeWriteBytes`) / period in seconds / 1,048,576
     38	- Average read latency in milliseconds per operation = Sum(`VolumeTotalReadTime`, in seconds) / Sum(`VolumeReadOps`) x 1,000 (and the write equivalent with `VolumeTotalWriteTime` and `VolumeWriteOps`). Without the x 1,000 the result is in seconds. Always state latency in milliseconds
     39	- Idle percentage = Sum(`VolumeIdleTime`) / period in seconds x 100
     40	- MiB/s from `VolumeAvgThroughput` = value in KiB/s / 1,024
     41	
     42	What a 1-minute average hides: sub-minute peaks can reach a limit while the minute average looks below it (micro-bursting). When latency or queue length rises while the average sits below the limit, say that headroom is not proven instead of claiming it.
     43	
     44	`EBSIOBalance%` and `EBSByteBalance%` are published only for some instance sizes (generally 4xlarge and smaller) that can burst. If they are absent, the instance does not publish them. That is not a fault.
     45	
     46	## Errors and fallbacks
     47	
     48	| What happens | What it means | What to do |
     49	|---|---|---|
     50	| `AccessDenied` on any call | The role cannot read that data | Name the exact API in Gaps. Continue with the rest |
     51	| A read call is held behind an operator-approval gate (for example `dlm:GetLifecyclePolicies` or `rbin:ListRules`) | The Agent Space treats it as an action | Report it as a Gap and say which conclusion stays unconfirmed. Never ask the operator to bypass the gate |
     52	| No `VolumeAvg*` data | The instance is not Nitro, or the `InstanceId` dimension is missing | Add `InstanceId`. If still empty, use the Sum-based math above |
     53	| `EBSIOBalance%` absent | The instance size does not publish it | Compare the summed IOPS and MiB/s of all attached volumes to the `DescribeInstanceTypes` baseline |
     54	| `DescribeInstanceTypes` values in MB/s | The API reports instance throughput in MB/s (bandwidth in Mbps) | Convert to MiB/s before comparing (1 MB/s = 1,000,000 bytes/s; 1 MiB/s = 1,048,576 bytes/s) |

Record a Gap for the modification history and for the 24-hour modification count |

     2	
     3	Load this file for any statement about how Amazon EBS behaves. Per-type limits are in [metrics-thresholds.md](metrics-thresholds.md).
     4	
     5	## Elastic Volumes rules
     6	
     7	- You can make up to 4 modifications to a volume in a rolling 24-hour period. There is no fixed waiting period between modifications; the next one is allowed once the previous one completes (January 2026 change).
     8	- Size can only increase. It cannot be reduced. To get a smaller volume, create a new volume and copy the data.
     9	- A modification request cannot be cancelled after it is submitted.
     10	- States are `modifying`, then `optimizing`, then `completed` (or `failed`). In `optimizing` the new configuration already applies, and performance is between the source and the target. The modification completes on its own.
     11	- Duration is best effort. The Amazon EBS User Guide says a 1 TiB volume typically takes up to about six hours to modify, and some performance changes take more than 24 hours, for example when the volume is not fully initialized.
     12	- After a size increase, the operating system must extend the partition and the file system. The agent gives the commands; the operator runs them.
     13	- Read the requirements page before proposing a change on an older instance, or on a volume with an MBR partition (2 TiB limit).
     14	
     15	## Instance EBS layer
     16	
     17	- All volumes attached to an instance share the instance's EBS bandwidth, IOPS and throughput. Sum the measured values across all attached volumes, including the root volume.
     18	- Size any target within the instance's EBS baseline from `DescribeInstanceTypes`, not its burst maximum.
     19	- `DescribeInstanceTypes` reports throughput in MB/s at 128 KiB I/O and IOPS at 16 KiB I/O. Convert MB/s to MiB/s before comparing with volume throughput.
     20	- Some smaller instance sizes burst above the baseline for a limited time and publish `EBSIOBalance%` and `EBSByteBalance%`. When those balances drain or reach 0, the instance drops to its baseline.
     21	
     22	## Quotas
     23	
     24	- Amazon EBS quotas are per Region. Check each Region the user works in.
     25	- Discover quota codes by name with `ListServiceQuotas --service-code ebs`. Never hardcode quota codes.
     26	- Read defaults from the Amazon EBS quotas page. For example, the default for snapshots per Region is 100,000 and it is adjustable.
     27	- The io2 regional IOPS quota is separate from the per-volume maximum. A request within the per-volume maximum can still fail on the regional quota. Existing io2 volumes already consume part of that quota.
     28	- Adjustable quotas are raised through Service Quotas. Quotas that are not adjustable need an AWS Support case.
     29	
     30	## Snapshots
     31	
     32	- Snapshots are incremental. Deleting a snapshot might not reduce storage cost, because later snapshots can reference its blocks. Any savings figure is an upper bound.
     33	- You cannot delete a snapshot that is the root device snapshot of a registered AMI, even if the AMI is deprecated or disabled. Deregister the AMI first, and only if it is no longer needed.
     34	- Snapshots created by AWS Backup are managed in AWS Backup, not with Amazon EC2 delete calls.
     35	- Identify Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager snapshots by `aws:dlm:*` tags, never by the snapshot name or description. A snapshot can be named like a DLM snapshot and still have no `aws:dlm:*` tags.
     36	- Target tags for Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager policies are case sensitive.
     37	- Recycle Bin rules decide whether a deleted snapshot can be recovered. With no matching rule, deletion is permanent.
     38	
     39	## Quirks that change answers
     40	
     41	| Quirk | Rule |
     42	|---|---|
     43	| `VolumeThroughputPercentage` on io1/io2 | Reports the percentage of provisioned IOPS delivered. Not a throughput signal |
     44	| `VolumeAvg*` metrics | Need `VolumeId` and `InstanceId`; Nitro only; `VolumeAvgThroughput` is KiB/s |
     45	| Change history | `DescribeVolumesModifications` returns only the most recent modification request per volume. Use it for the current or latest modification state. Earlier modifications and the 24-hour count come from AWS CloudTrail `ModifyVolume` events (optional, last 90 days); if unavailable, record a Gap |
     46	| Deletes | AWS DevOps Agent refuses delete-class operations, even with approval. Deletes are manual steps the customer runs with their own credentials, after the owner confirms |
     47	| Units | Throughput in MiB/s every time. Instance limits arrive in MB/s; convert |
     48	| Approval | A typed "approve" in chat is not approval. Only the approval card of a directed action approves a mutating action |

{"id": "f91ff2fa0cfe4673b22035681502aa74", "role": "user", "content": [{"text": "Fast agent report: a separate fast agent investigated this same incident in parallel and has finished. This is its whole final report, shared once. Nobody has checked it.

## Root cause
The bottleneck is the EBS volume's provisioned IOPS. A write workload of small 8 KiB writes started on i-1234567890abcdef0_3 (c6i.xlarge) at about 16:15 UTC. From 16:20 it has held io2 volume vol-0123456789abcdef0 (10 GiB, 1,000 provisioned IOPS) at 1,000 write IOPS. That figure is completely flat (≈300,000 ops in every 5-minute window), which is what a capped volume looks like. Throughput is only about 8 MB/s, so bandwidth is not the limit. Because the volume is at its limit, I/Os wait in line: VolumeQueueLength rose from 0 to about 1.33 and stayed there, and average write latency is about 1.33 ms (VolumeTotalWriteTime ÷ ops). Those two numbers agree with each other (queue ≈ IOPS × latency), which confirms the queue comes from saturation rather than a fault. The instance has plenty of headroom: InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck and InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck stayed at 0, and both EBSIOBalance% and EBSByteBalance% stayed at 99%. A c6i.xlarge supports about 6,000 IOPS baseline, well above 1,000. What to change: raise the provisioned IOPS with ModifyVolume. Online modification works on io2 and needs no detach or downtime. io2 allows up to 500 IOPS per GiB, so this 10 GiB volume can go up to 5,000 IOPS. If you need more than that, increase the volume size as well. Keep the total for all volumes on the instance under its EBS limits (about 6,000 IOPS baseline, 40,000 burst for c6i.xlarge), or change to a larger instance. You could also reduce IOPS demand by batching or coalescing the small 8 KiB writes into larger ones. Once you raise IOPS, raise the alarm threshold as well, because a queue length of about 1.3 at the cap is the expected steady state.
## Evidence
- ec2 DescribeVolumes: vol-0123456789abcdef0 is io2, 10 GiB, 1,000 provisioned IOPS, attached to i-1234567890abcdef0_3 at /dev/sdf.
- ec2 DescribeInstances: the instance is a c6i.xlarge (Nitro; about 6,000 IOPS / 156 MB/s baseline EBS).
- CloudWatch AWS/EBS VolumeWriteOps (5-min Sum): 0 from 15:50 to 16:10, 45,103 at 16:15, then 299,999 / 300,002 / 300,015 / 299,989 / 299,994 for 16:20–16:40. That is exactly 1,000 IOPS, the provisioned limit.
- AWS/EBS VolumeWriteBytes: about 2.4576 GB per 5 minutes, which works out to about 8.2 MB/s and 8 KiB per I/O. Throughput is far below io2 limits.
- AWS/EBS VolumeQueueLength: 0 before 16:15, then a steady 1.333–1.338 from 16:20. Alarm example-a-io2-queue-length (threshold 1.0) went to ALARM at 16:23:04 UTC.
- AWS/EBS VolumeTotalWriteTime: about 400 s per 300,000 ops, an average write latency of about 1.33 ms (1,000 IOPS × 1.33 ms ≈ queue depth 1.33).
- AWS/EC2 InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck and InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck: 0 for the whole period from 15:50 to 16:45.
- AWS/EC2 EBSIOBalance% and EBSByteBalance% (Minimum): 99% throughout, so the instance's burst allowance was never used.
- AWS/EC2 EBSWriteOps for the instance (about 300,300 per 5 minutes) almost exactly matches this volume's write ops, so this volume carries nearly all the instance's write I/O.
## Affected resources
- vol-0123456789abcdef0 (io2, example-a-io2)
- i-1234567890abcdef0_3 (c6i.xlarge)
- CloudWatch alarm example-a-io2-queue-length
## Gaps
- AWS/EBS VolumeIOPSExceededCheck returned no datapoints, so the cap is shown by the flat 1,000 IOPS against the provisioned value rather than by that metric.
- I did not identify which process or application started the write workload at about 16:15 UTC (no in-guest or application logs were checked).
- I did not check CloudTrail for recent ModifyVolume calls; the current configuration of 1,000 IOPS is what matches the observed ceiling.", "type": "text"}], "user_reference": null}

{"id": "471ae990-9924-436b-a8d6-8286e15f0a9d", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"thinking": "Time to wrap up with a clear verdict for the user, laying out the answer, supporting evidence, the binding layer, a recommendation, and any separate findings or gaps worth flagging.

", "signature": "", "type": "thinking"}, {"text": "The volume is the binding constraint. vol-0123456789abcdef0 is held at exactly its 1,000 provisioned IOPS, and the instance and AWS-side checks show nothing wrong. Raise the volume's provisioned IOPS to **3,000**. The instance's bandwidth limit makes about 3,000 the ceiling.

**Evidence** (AWS/EBS metrics, 16:20–16:47 UTC unless noted)
- **Volume config:** io2, 10 GiB, 1,000 provisioned IOPS, attached at /dev/sdf.
- **IOPS:** flat at 1,000.0 from 16:20. Before that there was no I/O at all (0 IOPS until about 16:19).
- **Workload:** 100% writes at 8 KiB each, so throughput is only 7.81 MiB/s. That is about 3% of the 256 MiB/s throughput limit io2 gives at 1,000 IOPS, so throughput is not the problem.
- **Built-in limit checks:** `VolumeIOPSExceededCheck` = 1 in every 5-minute window from 16:15 on. The throughput version of that check stayed at 0.
- **Queue and latency:** queue length went from 0 to about 1.33. Write latency is about 1.33 ms, from both `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` and total write time ÷ write ops. AWS documents under 0.5 ms for io2 Block Express.
- **Idle time:** about 0%, so writes were waiting the whole time.
- **Alarm:** `example-a-io2-queue-length` went to ALARM at 16:23:04.

**Instance layer has headroom** (c6i.xlarge)
- Its EBS baseline is 6,000 IOPS and 156.25 MB/s (149.01 MiB/s).
- All four attached volumes together used about 1,501 IOPS and 132.9 MiB/s (16:25–16:45).
- `EBSIOBalance%` and `EBSByteBalance%` stayed at 99%. Both instance-level "limit exceeded" checks stayed at 0.

**Not a fault:**
- Volume status is ok and `VolumeStalledIOCheck` is 0.
- There are no open AWS Health events for EBS or EC2.
- The only running fault-injection (FIS) experiment, EXP1234567890abcdef_7, adds latency to a different volume (vol-1234567890abcdef0_11) that isn't attached to this instance.
- This io2 volume has no recent modification.

**Root cause:** a new 8 KiB write workload started at about 16:19 UTC and needs more than the 1,000 IOPS provisioned. Writes queue at the cap, and that wait is the extra latency.

**Recommendation:** raise vol-0123456789abcdef0 from 1,000 to **3,000 IOPS** (keep io2, 10 GiB). It's an online change with no detach.
- **Why 3,000:** gp3 vol-1234567890abcdef0_18 already uses about 125.1 MiB/s of the instance's 149.01 MiB/s baseline. That leaves about 23.9 MiB/s, or about 3,060 IOPS at 8 KiB.
- **After the change:** the instance total would be about 3,501 IOPS and 148.5 MiB/s. That's within the baseline but close to it.
- **Volume limits:** io2 allows up to 1,000 IOPS per GiB (10,000 here). The volume's throughput limit becomes 768 MiB/s.
- **If you need more than about 3,000 IOPS:** the instance becomes the limit. Either move to c6i.2xlarge (12,000 IOPS and 298.02 MiB/s baseline) or reduce the gp3 volume's throughput use.
- **Cost:** goes up with provisioned IOPS.
- **Rollback:** set IOPS back to 1,000 once the change completes. A volume allows up to 4 changes in 24 hours.
- **Alarm:** review the queue-length threshold of 1.0 afterwards.
- **Another option:** batch the 8 KiB writes into larger ones to cut IOPS demand.

**Other things I found (they don't change the answer)**
- gp3 vol-1234567890abcdef0_18 is at its own 125 MiB/s limit, and its alarm `example-b-gp3-read-bytes` is also firing. It shares the instance bandwidth.
- vol-1234567890abcdef0_15 was lowered from 6,000 to 3,000 IOPS and from 250 to 125 MiB/s (08:42–10:49 UTC). It is idle now.

**Not checked**
- Which process started the writes at about 16:19. I had no in-guest or application logs.
- How many IOPS the workload actually wants. The cap hides it, so watch the volume after the change.
- Older volume change history in CloudTrail. I only checked the latest change per volume.

A separate step is drafting the volume change. It doesn't make the change on its own: it has to be approved on the approval card in the Operator Web App before it runs.", "type": "text"}], "user_reference": null}

{"id": "b42d42c3cfb7498f95065c26778fca44", "role": "user", "content": [{"text": "The background Task subagent assigned to task "propose-mitigation" successfully completed:

## Results
I'm proposing an online IOPS increase on the io2 volume **vol-0123456789abcdef0**, from 1,000 to 3,000 IOPS. Nothing has been changed; the plan below is for an engineer to run. It passed the safe-deployment policy check with no violations.

## What to do and why

**Action:** Change only the IOPS on the volume, in account 012345678901_1, us-east-1. Size (10 GiB) and type (io2) stay the same. Elastic Volumes applies this while the volume stays attached, so there is no detach, reboot or downtime.

**Why:**
- **The volume's own IOPS is the cap.** The 8 KiB, 100%-write workload that started at about 16:19Z has held the volume flat at exactly 1,000 IOPS since then. That has kept the queue at about 1.33 and write latency at about 1.33 ms, which is what keeps the alarm `example-a-io2-queue-length` in ALARM.
- **The instance has room.** Instance `i-1234567890abcdef0_3` (c6i.xlarge) has headroom. Throughput is not the limit.

**Why 3,000 IOPS:**
- **Volume limit:** io2 allows up to 1,000 IOPS per GiB, so this 10 GiB volume can go to 10,000 IOPS. At 3,000 IOPS its throughput limit is 768 MiB/s.
- **Instance limit:** the instance EBS baseline is 6,000 IOPS and 149.01 MiB/s. At 3,000 IOPS the instance total would be about 3,501 IOPS and 148.5 MiB/s. That fits, but it is close to the 149.01 MiB/s limit, because gp3 vol-1234567890abcdef0_18 alone uses about 125 MiB/s.
- **Going higher:** about 3,060 IOPS at 8 KiB is the most the instance can take today.

**What I checked now:**
- `DescribeVolumes`: io2, 10 GiB, Iops=1000, in-use, attached at /dev/sdf, Multi-Attach off.
- `DescribeVolumesModifications`: this volume has never been modified.
- CloudTrail: no `ModifyVolume` events for the volume in the last 24 hours. All 4 modifications allowed per rolling 24 hours are available. 3 remain after this change, and 2 if you also roll it back.
- The alarm has no actions configured: it doesn't page anyone or trigger automation.

## Execution plan

### 1. Prepare
1. **Save the current configuration as the rollback baseline.**
   ```
   aws ec2 describe-volumes --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1 > vol-0123456789abcdef0-baseline.json
   ```
   Check that it shows VolumeType=io2, Size=10, Iops=1000.

### 2. Pre-validate
1. **Make sure no modification is in progress.**
   ```
   aws ec2 describe-volumes-modifications --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1
   ```
   You should get `InvalidVolumeModification.NotFound` or a `completed` record. Stop if the state is `modifying` or `optimizing`.
2. **Check the volume is still pinned at its limit.** Run this with the last 15 minutes as the time range:
   ```
   aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace AWS/EBS --metric-name VolumeQueueLength --dimensions Name=VolumeId,Value=vol-0123456789abcdef0 --statistics Average --period 60 --start-time <now-15m> --end-time <now>
   ```
   Go ahead only if:
   - The queue is still about 1.33.
   - `VolumeWriteOps` is still about 60,000 per minute (1,000 IOPS).

### 3. Apply
1. **Raise the provisioned IOPS to 3,000.**
   ```
   aws ec2 modify-volume --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --iops 3000 --region us-east-1
   ```
   - **Expected states:** `modifying`, then `optimizing`, then `completed`. The new IOPS already applies during `optimizing`.
   - **Cost:** the bill goes up for 2,000 more provisioned io2 IOPS. At the usual us-east-1 price that is roughly $130 per month; check current pricing.
   - **Instance headroom:** instance throughput will be about 99.7% of the c6i.xlarge baseline. If gp3 vol-1234567890abcdef0_18 uses more throughput, or the io2 I/O size grows above 8 KiB, the instance becomes the cap instead.

### 4. Post-validate
1. **Follow the modification.**
   ```
   aws ec2 describe-volumes-modifications --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1
   ```
   Check TargetIops=3000 and the state moving to `optimizing` or `completed`.
2. **Confirm the new configuration.**
   ```
   aws ec2 describe-volumes --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1 --query 'Volumes[0].[VolumeType,Size,Iops,State]'
   ```
   You should see `io2, 10, 3000, in-use`.
3. **Confirm the volume is no longer capped and the instance still has room.** Over the 30 minutes after the change:
   - `VolumeIOPSExceededCheck` (AWS/EBS) should be 0.
   - Write IOPS should be either below 3,000 or settled at a new level.
   - `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` and application write latency should fall.
   - `InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck` and `InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck` should be 0.
   - `EBSByteBalance%` should hold near 99%.

   For example:
   ```
   aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace AWS/EC2 --metric-name InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck --dimensions Name=InstanceId,Value=i-1234567890abcdef0_3 --statistics Maximum --period 300 --start-time <now-30m> --end-time <now>
   ```

**If the workload climbs to about 3,000 IOPS and the volume caps again,** the instance baseline is the next limit. Don't raise the volume IOPS further. Instead, either:
- move to c6i.2xlarge (12,000 IOPS / 298.02 MiB/s), which needs a stop/start and a separate change, or
- reduce how much throughput gp3 vol-1234567890abcdef0_18 uses.

### 5. Rollback
1. **Set the IOPS back to 1,000 if you need to**, for example if instance-level contention appears or the extra capacity isn't needed:
   ```
   aws ec2 modify-volume --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --iops 1000 --region us-east-1
   ```
   You can only do this once the first change has reached `optimizing` or `completed`. It counts toward the 4 modifications per rolling 24 hours. Size and type are unchanged, so nothing else needs reverting.

## Durable fix (configuration / infrastructure as code)

1. **Keep the new IOPS in the volume's source definition.** If vol-0123456789abcdef0 is managed by IaC (CloudFormation, CDK or Terraform), set Iops=3000 there for the `example-a-io2` volume, so the next deploy doesn't revert it to 1,000.
   - The template shows Iops 3000, VolumeType io2, Size 10.
   - A redeploy or drift check shows no IOPS drift.
2. **Review the alarm threshold.** At the new rate, a VolumeQueueLength of about 1.33 is normal for this workload, so the `> 1.0` threshold would flag healthy operation. Alert on actual saturation instead.
   - Alarm on `VolumeIOPSExceededCheck` = 1, or on `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` above an agreed SLO, rather than queue length alone.
   - If queue length stays as the signal, base its threshold on the measured steady state after the change.
   - The alarm stays OK during normal load at 3,000 IOPS and fires when the volume's IOPS is exceeded.
3. **Add an instance-level alarm.** Instance `i-1234567890abcdef0_3` will run close to its EBS throughput baseline, so alarm on `InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck` and `EBSByteBalance%`. That way the next limit is caught early.
   - The alarms exist and fire when the instance goes over its baseline or the balance drops below an agreed level.

## What this plan doesn't cover
- **The workload's real demand is unknown.** While the volume caps it, it can't be measured. If it needs much more than about 3,000 IOPS, this change helps only partly, and the instance-type or gp3 throughput options above become necessary.
- **The source of the writes isn't confirmed.** It is still unknown which in-guest process started the 8 KiB writes at about 16:19Z. If that load was unexpected, the owner should decide whether to keep it or throttle it.
- **The gp3 volume's alarm is out of scope.** The separate alarm `example-b-gp3-read-bytes` (gp3 vol-1234567890abcdef0_18 at its own 125 MiB/s limit) is not addressed here. Raising that volume's throughput would push the instance past its EBS baseline.

# Investigation Summary

## Symptoms

### io2 volume queue length above alarm threshold
**Description:** Alarm example-a-io2-queue-length (VolumeQueueLength Average > 1.0, 60s period, 3 of 3 datapoints) entered ALARM at 2026-11-23 16:23:04 UTC. Queue length was 0 until 16:18, 0.99 at 16:19, and has held at 1.33–1.34 since 16:20. Write latency is a steady ~1.33 ms. VolumeStalledIOCheck = 0 throughout. Volume: vol-0123456789abcdef0 (io2, 10 GiB, 1000 IOPS, /dev/sdf) on i-1234567890abcdef0_3, account 012345678901_1, us-east-1.
**Time:** 2026-11-23T16:19:00Z

## Findings

### Root Cause: New 8 KiB write workload exceeds io2 volume's 1,000 provisioned IOPS
**Description:** A new 100%-write, 8 KiB workload began at ~16:19 UTC on i-1234567890abcdef0_3 and needs more than the 1,000 IOPS provisioned on io2 vol-0123456789abcdef0 ([redacted ARN], 10 GiB, /dev/sdf). From 16:20 IOPS is flat at 1,000.0, VolumeIOPSExceededCheck = 1, and idle time is ~0%. Writes queue at the cap: queue length is ~1.33 and write latency ~1.33 ms (AWS documents <0.5 ms for io2 Block Express). Throughput is 7.81 MiB/s, ~3% of the volume's limit. This is not a fault and not an instance limit: volume status is ok, stalled-IO is 0, there are no Health events, the running FIS experiment targets another volume, instance EBS checks are 0 and balances are 99%.
**Cascades to:** symptom-io2-queue-length

#### Supporting Observations
- **io2 volume holds a flat ~1000 write IOPS, equal to its provisioned IOPS:** From 16:20 UTC, vol-0123456789abcdef0 has sustained 999.7–1000.3 IOPS per minute, almost all writes; there are no reads after 16:19. The average I/O size is exactly 8 KiB and throughput is ~7.81 MiB/s, so bandwidth is not the constraint. VolumeIdleTime dropped from 60 s/min to ~0, so the device is busy the whole time. Write latency (VolumeTotalWriteTime ÷ ops) and VolumeAvgWriteLatency both read ~1.33 ms, consistent with the queue length of ~1.33. A plateau this flat at exactly 1000 IOPS is what a volume limited by its provisioned IOPS looks like.
- **VolumeIOPSExceededCheck = 1 on the io2 volume; instance-level checks stay 0:** For vol-0123456789abcdef0 on i-1234567890abcdef0_3, VolumeIOPSExceededCheck (5-min max) went from 0 to 1 in the 16:15 window and stayed at 1 through 16:45: demand exceeds the volume's provisioned 1000 IOPS. VolumeThroughputExceededCheck stayed 0. InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck and InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck stayed 0 throughout, so the instance is not throttling EBS.
- **Instance-wide EBS load ~1,501 IOPS / ~132.9 MiB/s, within c6i.xlarge baseline:** Over 16:25–16:45 UTC the four attached volumes together used ~1,501 IOPS and ~132.9 MiB/s, against the c6i.xlarge baseline of 6,000 IOPS and 156.25 MB/s (149.01 MiB/s). EBSIOBalance% and EBSByteBalance% stayed at 99%, and InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck and InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck stayed at 0. Most of the bandwidth (~125.1 MiB/s) belongs to gp3 vol-1234567890abcdef0_18, which leaves ~23.9 MiB/s (~3,060 IOPS at 8 KiB) of baseline headroom.
- **No FIS fault injection on this volume, no AWS Health events, and no recent change to the io2 volume:** The FIS experiments EXP1234567890abcdef_4 (16:15:35–16:19:24, stopped) and EXP1234567890abcdef_7 (running since 16:47) inject aws:ebs:volume-io-latency only on vol-1234567890abcdef0_11, which is not attached to this instance. - **All attached volumes report healthy status:** describe_volume_status shows Status=ok for all four volumes, with io-enabled=passed and io-performance=normal. #### Gaps
- **Source of the 16:19 write workload not identified:** No in-guest or application logs were available, so the process that started the 8 KiB writes on i-1234567890abcdef0_3 was not identified.
- **True IOPS demand masked by the cap:** Because the volume is pinned at 1,000 IOPS, the workload's real IOPS demand is unknown. Monitor vol-0123456789abcdef0 after raising IOPS to confirm that 3,000 is enough.

# Mitigation Summary

## Action
Raise provisioned IOPS on io2 volume vol-0123456789abcdef0 from 1,000 to 3,000 (online, no detach)

## Reasoning
The 8 KiB, 100%-write workload is capped at exactly the volume's 1,000 provisioned IOPS, which keeps queue length ~1.33 and the alarm in ALARM. The c6i.xlarge has IOPS headroom, but gp3 vol-1234567890abcdef0_18 already uses ~125 MiB/s of the 149.01 MiB/s instance baseline, leaving room for ~3,060 IOPS at 8 KiB, so 3,000 is the ceiling. Passed the safe-deployment policy check; all 4 modifications per 24 h are available.

## Execution Plan

### Step 1: Prepare

#### 1.1 Record the current configuration (io2, 10 GiB, 1000 IOPS) for rollback
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 describe-volumes --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1 > vol-0123456789abcdef0-baseline.json
```
**Purpose:** Record the current configuration (io2, 10 GiB, 1000 IOPS) for rollback

### Step 2: Pre Validate

#### 2.1 Make sure no modification is in progress
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 describe-volumes-modifications --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1
```
**Purpose:** Make sure no modification is in progress
**Risks:** Stop if the state is modifying or optimizing

#### 2.2 Confirm the queue is still ~1.33 and writes ~60,000/min before…
**Type:** command
```
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace AWS/EBS --metric-name VolumeQueueLength --dimensions Name=VolumeId,Value=vol-0123456789abcdef0 --statistics Average --period 60 --start-time <now-15m> --end-time <now>
```
**Purpose:** Confirm the queue is still ~1.33 and writes ~60,000/min before proceeding

### Step 3: Apply

#### 3.1 Lift the volume's IOPS cap online
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 modify-volume --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --iops 3000 --region us-east-1
```
**Purpose:** Lift the volume's IOPS cap online
**Risks:** Cost rises by ~2,000 provisioned io2 IOPS (roughly $130/month in us-east-1), Instance EBS throughput will sit at ~99.7% of the c6i.xlarge baseline
**Advisory:** If gp3 vol-1234567890abcdef0_18 uses more throughput or I/O size grows above 8 KiB, the instance becomes the cap

### Step 4: Post Validate

#### 4.1 Track TargetIops=3000 moving to optimizing or completed
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 describe-volumes-modifications --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1
```
**Purpose:** Track TargetIops=3000 moving to optimizing or completed

#### 4.2 Confirm io2, 10, 3000, in-use
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 describe-volumes --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1 --query 'Volumes[0].[VolumeType,Size,Iops,State]'
```
**Purpose:** Confirm io2, 10, 3000, in-use

#### 4.3 Confirm the instance stays within its EBS baseline
**Type:** command
```
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace AWS/EC2 --metric-name InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck --dimensions Name=InstanceId,Value=i-1234567890abcdef0_3 --statistics Maximum --period 300 --start-time <now-30m> --end-time <now>
```
**Purpose:** Confirm the instance stays within its EBS baseline
**Advisory:** Over 30 min also expect VolumeIOPSExceededCheck = 0, lower write latency, InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck = 0 and EBSByteBalance% near 99%, If the volume caps again near 3,000 IOPS, move to c6i.2xlarge or reduce gp3 throughput instead of raising IOPS further

### Step 5: Rollback

#### 5.1 Restore the original provisioned IOPS
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 modify-volume --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --iops 1000 --region us-east-1
```
**Purpose:** Restore the original provisioned IOPS
**Risks:** Only possible once the first change reaches optimizing or completed, Counts toward the 4 modifications per rolling 24 h

## Code Change Specification

### Requirements

#### 1. Codify the new IOPS in IaC
**Description:** If example-a-io2 is managed by CloudFormation, CDK or Terraform, set Iops=3000 so a redeploy does not revert it.
**Acceptance Criteria:**
- Template shows Iops 3000, VolumeType io2, Size 10
- Redeploy or drift check shows no IOPS drift

#### 2. Rework the queue-length alarm
**Description:** Queue length ~1.33 is normal for this workload, so the > 1.0 threshold flags healthy operation. Alarm on VolumeIOPSExceededCheck = 1 or VolumeAvgWriteLatency above an SLO, or rebase the threshold on post-change steady state.
**Acceptance Criteria:**
- Alarm stays OK under normal load at 3,000 IOPS
- Alarm fires when the volume's IOPS is exceeded

#### 3. Add instance-level EBS alarms
**Description:** Alarm on InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck and EBSByteBalance% for i-1234567890abcdef0_3, which will run near its EBS throughput baseline.
**Acceptance Criteria:**
- Alarms exist and fire when the instance exceeds its baseline or balance drops below an agreed level

Also ruled out: impairment and fault injection. Volume status was ok (io-enabled passed, io-performance normal), VolumeStalledIOCheck=0, there were no open AWS Health EBS/EC2 events, and the running FIS experiment EXP1234567890abcdef_7 targets a different volume (vol-1234567890abcdef0_11), not one attached to this instance. - Sizing constraint: The other volumes use about 125.09 MiB/s and 501.5 IOPS. That leaves about 23.9 MiB/s and 5,498 IOPS within the c6i.xlarge baseline for the io2 volume. At 8 KiB I/O, 23.9 MiB/s allows about 3,060 IOPS. A target of 3,000 IOPS on the io2 volume brings the instance total to about 3,501 IOPS and 148.5 MiB/s, which is within the baseline but close to the 149.01 MiB/s limit. io2 allows up to 1,000 IOPS per GiB, so 10 GiB allows up to 10,000 IOPS. 3,000 IOPS gives a 768 MiB/s volume throughput limit.      41	Do not use this skill for Amazon S3, Amazon EFS, Amazon FSx, instance store, or Amazon EC2 issues unrelated to Amazon EBS.
     42	
     43	## Prerequisites
     44	
     45	- Read-only permissions for the APIs listed in [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md).
     46	- AWS CloudTrail access is optional. The skill works without it.
     47	- Mutating changes run only through directed actions (Agent Actions in the Operator Web App), which need their own role and operator approval on the approval card.
     48	
     49	---
     50	
     51	## Workflow
     52	
     53	Copy this checklist and tick each step as you finish it:
     54	
     55	- [ ] Step 1: Classify the request
     56	- [ ] Step 2: Load the shared references
     57	- [ ] Step 3: Run the path and draft the report
     58	- [ ] Step 4: Check the draft, fix it, then present it
     59	
     60	## Step 1: Classify the Request
     61	
     62	| The user says or the alarm shows | Mode and path | Load |
     63	|---|---|---|
     64	| "My app is slow", high latency, an alarm on AWS/EBS metrics, `EBSIOBalance%` or `EBSByteBalance%`, "is it storage?", "how much IOPS do I need?" | Troubleshoot: performance | [references/troubleshoot-performance.md](references/troubleshoot-performance.md) |
     65	| "My modification is stuck", "the new IOPS has not taken effect", a `ModifyVolume` error, resize, gp2 to gp3, extend the file system, shrink or cancel | Troubleshoot: volume modification | [references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md](references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md) |
     66	| "Which snapshots can I delete?", snapshot copy did not arrive, AMI creation stuck, recover a deleted snapshot or volume, Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager, Recycle Bin | Troubleshoot: snapshots | [references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md](references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md) |

     73	If a request fits more than one row, answer the question the user asked first and treat the rest as Separate findings.
     74	
     75	## Step 2: Load the Shared References
     76	
     77	- Always load [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md) (read-only APIs, metric math, errors and fallbacks).
     78	- Load [references/metrics-thresholds.md](references/metrics-thresholds.md) for any metric judgement.
     79	- Load [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md) for the verdict, the binding layer, escalation and review ratings.

     81	
     82	## Step 3: Run the Path and Draft the Report
     83	
     84	Follow the numbered procedure in the loaded path. Discover every value from the APIs. Then draft the report in the format below.
     85	
     86	### Troubleshoot verdict format
     87	
     88	1. **Answer:** the asked question, answered first.
     89	2. **Evidence:** values with units and time window.
     90	3. **Binding layer:** Volume, Instance, Burst credits, Quota, Not EBS, AWS-side impairment (only with a direct signal, see [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md)), Indeterminate, or Not applicable.
     91	4. **Recommendation:** exact parameters, or "No change".
     92	5. **Separate findings:** other true facts that do not change the Answer.
     93	6. **Gaps:** what could not be checked and why.
     94	
     95	In an investigation, put the Answer and the Recommendation with its exact parameters in the root cause finding, not only under Gaps. Keep the findings on the resource the user asked about. Mention another volume only when it shares the same instance EBS baseline, and then as a Separate finding.
     96	
     97	When the Binding layer is Indeterminate, report it as one finding. Do not offer AWS-side impairment as a hypothesis. List each direct check you ran (volume status, `VolumeStalledIOCheck`, AWS Health, AWS FIS) with its result as supporting evidence, say that no check confirms or rules out an EBS-side slowdown, and give the escalation path.
     98	
     99	Review mode uses the rated report in [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md). Every Review mode response MUST begin with its Summary table, which rates all six areas (capacity and quota headroom, observability, cost hygiene, resilience, encryption posture, deletion protection), even when an area has no findings or is `Indeterminate`. The Summary table is required, not optional. Do not open with prose or an offer to run the review; start with the table, then the per-area detail.
     100	
     101	## Step 4: Check the Draft Before Presenting It
     102	
     103	Review the draft from Step 3 against these checks. Fix anything that fails, then present it.
     104	
     105	- Every number under Evidence came from an API call made in this session, has its unit and time window, and matches the resource ID it is attributed to.
     106	- The Binding layer agrees with the Evidence: the named layer is the one at its limit, and the other layers were checked and shown to have headroom. The Evidence gives the instance EBS baseline in MiB/s and IOPS next to the summed demand of all attached volumes.
     107	- Any Recommendation stays within the instance's EBS baseline and the volume type's documented limits, and it is not more provisioning for an impairment.
     108	- Every snapshot tier is backed by the checks it requires; if one of those checks failed, the item is not listed for owner review. No snapshot is recommended for deletion; the owner confirms first.
     109	- A review answer starts with the Summary table and rates all six areas.
     110	- Every API that failed or was not called is listed under Gaps.
     111	
     112	---
     113	
     114	## Critical Rules
     115	
     116	- **Read-only.** Changes (ModifyVolume, quota requests) are proposed with exact parameters, cost and rollback, and run only through operator-approved directed actions (Agent Actions in the Operator Web App). Approval is given only on the approval card. A typed "approve" in chat is not approval.
     117	- **Deletes are manual customer steps.** AWS DevOps Agent refuses delete-class operations (for example DeleteSnapshot, DeleteVolume, DeregisterImage), so never propose them as directed actions. After the owner confirms they no longer need the resource, give the commands for the customer to run with their own credentials.
     118	- **Answer in one reply.** In chat, run the checks in this conversation and return the finished verdict or report as your reply. Do not hand the work to a background sub-agent and reply with a "started" or "I will report back" message, because that message becomes the answer the user sees first.
     119	- **Discover, don't assume:** read every configuration value from the APIs.
     120	- **Rule EBS in or out before tuning it.**
     121	- **Answer the asked question first;** other findings go under "Separate findings".
     122	- **Review mode starts with the Summary table.** Every Review mode response begins with the Summary table of all six rated areas. The table is required, not optional.
     123	- **Always check the instance layer** and size changes within the instance's EBS **baseline**.
     124	- **Never recommend more provisioning for an impairment.**
     125	- **Use current service rules:** up to 4 Elastic Volumes modifications per volume per rolling 24 hours. There is no fixed waiting period between modifications; the next one is allowed once the previous one completes.
     126	- **No interpretation without data:** report what couldn't be checked and use fallbacks. `DescribeVolumesModifications` returns only the most recent modification per volume; modification history and counts come from the optional AWS CloudTrail `ModifyVolume` events, or are listed under Gaps.
     127	- **Units:** MiB/s for throughput, stated every time.
     128	- **Escalate** on scope signals or when the investigation can't explain the symptom.
     129	
     130	## Gotchas
     131	
     132	- A modification in `optimizing` is not stuck. The new size, IOPS or throughput already applies while it optimizes.
     133	- `DescribeInstanceTypes` reports EBS bandwidth in MB/s. Convert it to MiB/s before comparing it with volume throughput.
     134	- On io1 and io2, `VolumeThroughputPercentage` is the percentage of provisioned IOPS delivered. It is not a throughput signal.
     135	- `VolumeAvgIOPS`, `VolumeAvgThroughput`, `VolumeAvgReadLatency` and `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` need both `VolumeId` and `InstanceId` and exist only on Nitro instances. `VolumeAvgThroughput` is in KiB/s. `VolumeTotalReadTime` and `VolumeTotalWriteTime` are in seconds.
     136	- Rising latency and queue length with falling IOPS is not proof of an AWS-side impairment. Without a direct signal (failed `VolumeStalledIOCheck`, impaired volume status, or an open AWS Health event) and without a running AWS FIS experiment, the Binding layer is Indeterminate.
     137	- `DescribeVolumesModifications` returns only the latest modification per volume. It cannot count modifications in the last 24 hours.
     138	- `ListRecoveryPointsByResource` without `ManagedByAWSBackupOnly` set to true also lists snapshots that AWS Backup did not create.
     139	- A snapshot whose source volume is gone may be the only remaining copy of the data. List it for owner review; never call it safe to delete.
     140	- Snapshots are incremental, so deleting one may free less storage than its size suggests.
     141	
     142	## Error Handling
     143	
     144	Errors, gated reads and missing metrics are handled with the fallback table in [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md). Name every failed API under Gaps and continue with the rest.

{"id": "5aafdd29-0eb2-4f68-a2fe-5b4cb52c8bd5", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_01AHCt8Br6tB67xQUWBPxv", "content": [{"text": "     1	# Troubleshoot: Elastic Volumes modification
     2	
     3	## When this path applies
     4	
     5	- "My modification is stuck", "the new IOPS has not taken effect", "how long will optimizing take?"
     6	- A `ModifyVolume` call failed with an error.
     7	- Sizing a resize, an IOPS or throughput change, or a gp2 to gp3 migration.
     8	- Extending the file system after a size increase.
     9	- Shrinking a volume or cancelling a modification.
     10	
     11	## Procedure
     12	
     13	1. **Find the volume.** Use the volume ID the user gives, or discover it with `DescribeVolumes` (by instance attachment or by the volumes that have recent modifications). Never pick a volume by its Name tag alone; confirm the ID with the user if more than one matches.
     14	2. **Read the latest modification record.** `DescribeVolumesModifications` for the volume: `ModificationState`, `Progress`, original and target values (size, type, IOPS, throughput), `StartTime`, `EndTime`, `StatusMessage`. This API returns only the most recent modification request for each volume. Use it for the current or latest modification state, not for history.
     15	3. **Answer the asked question first, in plain words.**
     16	   - `modifying` or `optimizing`: not stuck. In `optimizing` the new configuration already applies and performance is between the source and the target. It completes on its own.
     17	   - `completed`: done. The new values apply.
     18	   - `failed`: read `StatusMessage` and translate it (step 5).
     19	   - Duration is best effort. The Amazon EBS User Guide says a 1 TiB volume typically takes up to about six hours to modify, and some performance changes take more than 24 hours, for example when the volume is not fully initialized.
     20	4. **Count the modifications in the rolling 24 hours.** Up to 4 per volume in a rolling 24-hour period. There is no fixed waiting period between modifications; the next one is allowed once the previous one completes. `DescribeVolumesModifications` cannot give this count, because it returns only the latest modification. Count the `ModifyVolume` events for the volume in the last 24 hours with the optional AWS CloudTrail `LookupEvents` call (filter on the volume ID as the resource name, or on the event name `ModifyVolume`). Report how many remain in the current window. As a cross-check, the latest record from step 2 should appear among those events if its `StartTime` is in the last 24 hours. If the lookup is denied or unavailable, record a Gap ("the number of modifications in the last 24 hours could not be confirmed") and do not state how many remain.
     21	5. **Translate errors.**
     22	   - io2 "Iops to volume size ratio of ... is too high; maximum is 1000": io2 allows up to 1,000 IOPS per GiB. To reach the target IOPS, the size must be at least target IOPS / 1,000 GiB. Propose that size together with the IOPS.
     23	   - gp3: up to 500 IOPS per GiB, and throughput up to 0.25 MiB/s per provisioned IOPS. If a request breaks either rule, give the size or IOPS that satisfies it.
     24	   - Size decrease: not allowed. Size can only increase. To get a smaller volume, create a new volume and copy the data.
     25	   - Cancel: a submitted modification cannot be cancelled. Wait for it to complete; a reverse change then counts toward the 4 in 24 hours.
     26	   - Limit reached: the 4 modifications in the window are used. The next one is possible when the oldest falls out of the rolling 24-hour window.
     27	   - Older instance types or MBR volumes: check the Elastic Volumes requirements page.
     28	6. **Size a new target.**
     29	   - Keep it within the instance's remaining EBS baseline: `DescribeInstanceTypes` baseline (converted to MiB/s) minus the measured usage of the other attached volumes.
     30	   - gp2 to gp3: keep at least the gp2 volume's current baseline IOPS (3 x GiB, minimum 100) and its measured throughput. gp3 includes 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s at any size; provision more only if measured demand needs it.
     31	   - State how the target was computed.
     32	7. **File system extension after a size increase.** Give the commands for the operator to run on the instance. Never execute them.
     33	   - `lsblk` to see the device and partition
     34	   - `sudo growpart /dev/<device> <partition-number>` if the volume has a partition
     35	   - `sudo xfs_growfs -d <mount-point>` for XFS, or `sudo resize2fs /dev/<device-or-partition>` for ext4
     36	   - Point to the extend-the-file-system guide for Windows and other cases.
     37	8. **Separate findings.** If the instance caps what the volume can deliver, write that under Separate findings. Never phrase it as "the modification failed" when the record shows `optimizing` or `completed`.
     38	
     39	## Decision rules
     40	
     41	- The modification record decides the Answer. Performance metrics never override it.
     42	- An instance ceiling is a Separate finding with its own recommendation (instance type change).
     43	- Use the binding-layer tree in [finding-logic.md](finding-logic.md) only when the user also asks about performance.
     44	
     45	## What to report
     46	
     47	The verdict template in [finding-logic.md](finding-logic.md). The Answer names the state and what it means. Evidence lists the record fields. Recommendation gives the exact next call, if any. Gaps list anything unreadable.
     48	
     49	## Safety rules
     50	
     51	- The agent never runs `ModifyVolume` on its own. It proposes it as a directed action, approved on the approval card. A typed "approve" in chat is not approval.
     52	- The proposal includes: the exact call (`--volume-id`, and only the changed fields among `--size`, `--volume-type`, `--iops`, `--throughput`), the expected state sequence (`modifying`, `optimizing`, `completed`), how many of the 4 modifications in the rolling 24 hours remain after this change (only when step 4 confirmed the count; otherwise say it is unconfirmed), cost direction, and rollback.
     53	- Rollback: after the change completes, a reverse change of IOPS, throughput or type is possible and counts toward the 4. Size cannot roll back.
     54	- Recommend a snapshot before a type change or a large resize on a volume with data the user cannot lose.

{"id": "83d973a9-8828-4f33-9167-f11e51dd8f65", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "I'm proposing an online IOPS increase on the io2 volume **vol-0123456789abcdef0**, from 1,000 to 3,000 IOPS. Nothing has been changed; the plan below is for an engineer to run. It passed the safe-deployment policy check with no violations.

## What to do and why

**Action:** Change only the IOPS on the volume, in account 012345678901_1, us-east-1. Size (10 GiB) and type (io2) stay the same. Elastic Volumes applies this while the volume stays attached, so there is no detach, reboot or downtime.

**Why:**
- **The volume's own IOPS is the cap.** The 8 KiB, 100%-write workload that started at about 16:19Z has held the volume flat at exactly 1,000 IOPS since then. That has kept the queue at about 1.33 and write latency at about 1.33 ms, which is what keeps the alarm `example-a-io2-queue-length` in ALARM.
- **The instance has room.** Instance `i-1234567890abcdef0_3` (c6i.xlarge) has headroom. Throughput is not the limit.

**Why 3,000 IOPS:**
- **Volume limit:** io2 allows up to 1,000 IOPS per GiB, so this 10 GiB volume can go to 10,000 IOPS. At 3,000 IOPS its throughput limit is 768 MiB/s.
- **Instance limit:** the instance EBS baseline is 6,000 IOPS and 149.01 MiB/s. At 3,000 IOPS the instance total would be about 3,501 IOPS and 148.5 MiB/s. That fits, but it is close to the 149.01 MiB/s limit, because gp3 vol-1234567890abcdef0_18 alone uses about 125 MiB/s.
- **Going higher:** about 3,060 IOPS at 8 KiB is the most the instance can take today.

**What I checked now:**
- `DescribeVolumes`: io2, 10 GiB, Iops=1000, in-use, attached at /dev/sdf, Multi-Attach off.
- `DescribeVolumesModifications`: this volume has never been modified.
- CloudTrail: no `ModifyVolume` events for the volume in the last 24 hours. All 4 modifications allowed per rolling 24 hours are available. 3 remain after this change, and 2 if you also roll it back.
- The alarm has no actions configured: it doesn't page anyone or trigger automation.

## Execution plan

### 1. Prepare
1. **Save the current configuration as the rollback baseline.**
   ```
   aws ec2 describe-volumes --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1 > vol-0123456789abcdef0-baseline.json
   ```
   Check that it shows VolumeType=io2, Size=10, Iops=1000.

### 2. Pre-validate
1. **Make sure no modification is in progress.**
   ```
   aws ec2 describe-volumes-modifications --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1
   ```
   You should get `InvalidVolumeModification.NotFound` or a `completed` record. Stop if the state is `modifying` or `optimizing`.
2. **Check the volume is still pinned at its limit.** Run this with the last 15 minutes as the time range:
   ```
   aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace AWS/EBS --metric-name VolumeQueueLength --dimensions Name=VolumeId,Value=vol-0123456789abcdef0 --statistics Average --period 60 --start-time <now-15m> --end-time <now>
   ```
   Go ahead only if:
   - The queue is still about 1.33.
   - `VolumeWriteOps` is still about 60,000 per minute (1,000 IOPS).

### 3. Apply
1. **Raise the provisioned IOPS to 3,000.**
   ```
   aws ec2 modify-volume --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --iops 3000 --region us-east-1
   ```
   - **Expected states:** `modifying`, then `optimizing`, then `completed`. The new IOPS already applies during `optimizing`.
   - **Cost:** the bill goes up for 2,000 more provisioned io2 IOPS. At the usual us-east-1 price that is roughly $130 per month; check current pricing.
   - **Instance headroom:** instance throughput will be about 99.7% of the c6i.xlarge baseline. If gp3 vol-1234567890abcdef0_18 uses more throughput, or the io2 I/O size grows above 8 KiB, the instance becomes the cap instead.

### 4. Post-validate
1. **Follow the modification.**
   ```
   aws ec2 describe-volumes-modifications --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1
   ```
   Check TargetIops=3000 and the state moving to `optimizing` or `completed`.
2. **Confirm the new configuration.**
   ```
   aws ec2 describe-volumes --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1 --query 'Volumes[0].[VolumeType,Size,Iops,State]'
   ```
   You should see `io2, 10, 3000, in-use`.
3. **Confirm the volume is no longer capped and the instance still has room.** Over the 30 minutes after the change:
   - `VolumeIOPSExceededCheck` (AWS/EBS) should be 0.
   - Write IOPS should be either below 3,000 or settled at a new level.
   - `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` and application write latency should fall.
   - `InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck` and `InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck` should be 0.
   - `EBSByteBalance%` should hold near 99%.

   For example:
   ```
   aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace AWS/EC2 --metric-name InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck --dimensions Name=InstanceId,Value=i-1234567890abcdef0_3 --statistics Maximum --period 300 --start-time <now-30m> --end-time <now>
   ```

**If the workload climbs to about 3,000 IOPS and the volume caps again,** the instance baseline is the next limit. Don't raise the volume IOPS further. Instead, either:
- move to c6i.2xlarge (12,000 IOPS / 298.02 MiB/s), which needs a stop/start and a separate change, or
- reduce how much throughput gp3 vol-1234567890abcdef0_18 uses.

### 5. Rollback
1. **Set the IOPS back to 1,000 if you need to**, for example if instance-level contention appears or the extra capacity isn't needed:
   ```
   aws ec2 modify-volume --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --iops 1000 --region us-east-1
   ```
   You can only do this once the first change has reached `optimizing` or `completed`. It counts toward the 4 modifications per rolling 24 hours. Size and type are unchanged, so nothing else needs reverting.

## Durable fix (configuration / infrastructure as code)

1. **Keep the new IOPS in the volume's source definition.** If vol-0123456789abcdef0 is managed by IaC (CloudFormation, CDK or Terraform), set Iops=3000 there for the `example-a-io2` volume, so the next deploy doesn't revert it to 1,000.
   - The template shows Iops 3000, VolumeType io2, Size 10.
   - A redeploy or drift check shows no IOPS drift.
2. **Review the alarm threshold.** At the new rate, a VolumeQueueLength of about 1.33 is normal for this workload, so the `> 1.0` threshold would flag healthy operation. Alert on actual saturation instead.
   - Alarm on `VolumeIOPSExceededCheck` = 1, or on `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` above an agreed SLO, rather than queue length alone.
   - If queue length stays as the signal, base its threshold on the measured steady state after the change.
   - The alarm stays OK during normal load at 3,000 IOPS and fires when the volume's IOPS is exceeded.
3. **Add an instance-level alarm.** Instance `i-1234567890abcdef0_3` will run close to its EBS throughput baseline, so alarm on `InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck` and `EBSByteBalance%`. That way the next limit is caught early.
   - The alarms exist and fire when the instance goes over its baseline or the balance drops below an agreed level.

## What this plan doesn't cover
- **The workload's real demand is unknown.** While the volume caps it, it can't be measured. If it needs much more than about 3,000 IOPS, this change helps only partly, and the instance-type or gp3 throughput options above become necessary.
- **The source of the writes isn't confirmed.** It is still unknown which in-guest process started the 8 KiB writes at about 16:19Z. If that load was unexpected, the owner should decide whether to keep it or throttle it.
- **The gp3 volume's alarm is out of scope.** The separate alarm `example-b-gp3-read-bytes` (gp3 vol-1234567890abcdef0_18 at its own 125 MiB/s limit) is not addressed here. Raising that volume's throughput would push the instance past its EBS baseline.", "type": "text"}], "user_reference": null}
